title: Redwood Structured Output & Function Calling Demo
next_steps: Provide pricing estimate for Dedicated capacity
Schedule 2-week POC kickoff with Markus and Carlos
action_items: Maya Patel: Share demo recording and slides by 2025-06-11
Carlos Nguyen: Prepare POC scope doc and runbook by 2025-06-13
Markus Jansen: Share sample prompt set and traffic profile by 2025-06-12
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a product walkthrough showing Structured JSON output (JSON mode), schema enforcement and function/tool calling. Discussed integration patterns, guardrails in Console, Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization, and enterprise security (SOC 2, KMS, audit logs). Customer is interested in a 2-week POC on Dedicated capacity to validate latency and structured output reliability.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the Redwood side and with me is Carlos, our solutions engineer. Um, quick check, do you see my screen?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we can see it. Thanks, Maya.
[00:11] Maya Patel: Great. Quick agenda — structured output demo, JSON mode, function (uh) calling examples, Console guardrails and then Q&A.
[00:20] Carlos Nguyen: Hi all — I'll jump into the demo parts. Markus, Priya, good to meet you.
[00:25] Markus Jansen: Hey, thanks. We're mostly focused on reliability of structured outputs, and how that maps to our downstream systems.
[00:33] Priya Singh: And from privacy side, we'll want to confirm data residency and KMS integration.
[00:38] Maya Patel: Totally. We'll cover those. Quick note — this is a recorded session and I'll share the slides afterwards.
[00:46] Carlos Nguyen: Alright I'm switching to the Console. First slide, JSON mode — this is what many teams use when they need a strict schema output so it's machine parseable.
[00:56] [01:00] Carlos Nguyen: In the Console you can define a schema, for example a simple payment intent with fields: intent_id, amount_cents, currency, merchant_id, and a metadata object. You can enforce types and required fields.
[01:14] Markus Jansen: When you say enforce — does the runtime reject responses that don't follow the schema or does it attempt to coerce?
[01:21] Carlos Nguyen: Good question. We have a couple modes. By default Redwood will try to coerce and return a parseable JSON, with a confidence score and any schema violations in a structured error block. There's also a strict mode that will trigger a fallback policy, so you can route those requests to a secondary model or to a human review queue.
[01:37] [01:40] Lena Ortiz: Is that strict mode available on Hosted as well as Dedicated?
[01:44] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, same API semantics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments — that's one of our differentiators.
[01:51] Maya Patel: Also worth noting, the SDKs return typed output, so in Node/Python it's easy to deserialize and fail-fast.
[01:58] [02:00] Carlos Nguyen: Ok next — function calling. Here we're going to show a sample where the model returns a JSON payload that maps directly to an internal webhook to create a payment. I'll run the request now.
[02:09] [02:15] Carlos Nguyen: (typing) Sending... you can see the response stream; it's emitting the structured fields as tokens but the Console aggregates into the final JSON.
[02:25] [02:30] Carlos Nguyen: Response — intent_id: "pay_20250610_01", amount_cents: 1250, currency: "USD", merchant_id: "m_6721". There's also a _redwood_meta block with schema_validation: true and model_confidence: 0.92.
[02:45] Markus Jansen: That _redwood_meta helps a lot. We can wire that to our consumer to flag low confidence items.
[02:50] Priya Singh: And audit logs — are those available for these calls? We need traceability for payment events.
[02:56] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — all requests have per-request audit events captured. If you're on Dedicated/Private you can route logs to your SIEM or enable longer retention in the Console. We integrate with common KMS providers for envelope encryption.
[03:08] [03:15] Lena Ortiz: What about latency? If we enforce strict schema and do validation, what's the impact?
[03:20] Carlos Nguyen: Minimal usually — schema validation is local and fast. The bigger latency drivers are model selection and batching. For example in Dedicated we can guarantee p95 latency targets and we support single-request low-latency paths or batched throughput-optimized paths. Redwood Optimize will recommend batching parameters based on your request distribution.
[03:37] Maya Patel: I can show a Optimize suggestion — Carlos, jump to the Optimize panel.
[03:42] [03:45] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. Here the Optimize tab analyzed sample traffic and suggests a batch size of 8 for best cost/latency tradeoff, and recommends a quantized model variant (q4_0) for non-critical outputs. You can pin a high-accuracy model for strict schema calls and a cheaper variant for best-effort tasks.
[03:59] Markus Jansen: Do you support automatic fallback between variants if capacity is constrained?
[04:04] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — Smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants or other regions. You control the policy: cost-first, latency-first, or strict.
[04:12] [04:20] Lena Ortiz: Can you demo an example where the model calls a tool — like calling our own invoice service?
[04:26] Carlos Nguyen: Yep. I'll switch to a function-calling example. In the request we register a tool endpoint and a JSON schema for the payload the tool expects. When the model returns a call, Redwood validates the payload and, depending on your policy, can either call the webhook automatically or surface the payload for review.
[04:44] [04:50] Carlos Nguyen: (typing) Ok sending a sample prompt: "Create payment for order 9923". Response streaming... the model emits a function_call object with name: "create_payment" and arguments matching our schema.
[05:05] Priya Singh: For automatic calls — what's the security model? We don't want arbitrary calls to our internal endpoints.
[05:11] Carlos Nguyen: We recommend setting up a short-lived signed token and IP allowlist. On Dedicated/Private you can use VPC peering, and mutual TLS between Redwood agent and your endpoint. The Console also allows a manual approval workflow.
[05:24] Maya Patel: Also, you can configure guardrails so only approved function names are allowed and set rate limits per function.
[05:32] [05:40] Lena Ortiz: Any examples of schema failures and how they're surfaced?
[05:43] Carlos Nguyen: Yep — here's an example where amount_cents is returned as a string. The Console shows a schema_violations pane with the original model output, the coerced result, and a flag. You can set a policy to reject, coerce, or fallback.
[05:59] Markus Jansen: In our stack we deserialize into a strictly typed proto. Coercion sometimes hides bugs. We prefer strict rejection and human review for high-value payments.
[06:10] Maya Patel: Makes sense. For payment flows you likely want strict mode and a canary rollout. Redwood supports canary percentages by route so you can start with 5% of traffic using model XYZ.
[06:21] [06:30] Carlos Nguyen: Quick demo — I'm toggling the route to strict mode and kicking a few test requests. You can see that failing request is routed to the human-review queue with a link to a manual approve UI.
[06:45] Priya Singh: Nice. On data residency — we have EU customers, and data must not cross regions.
[06:50] Carlos Nguyen: With Dedicated you can pin a region and with Private you control the network. We also support customer-managed keys — your encryption keys never leave your KMS.
[06:59] [07:10] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk about costs — how does structured output affect token billing?
[07:16] Maya Patel: Structured output doesn't change token accounting — you still pay for generation tokens. But by constraining outputs to shorter, schema-driven responses you often reduce tokens overall. Also batching and caching reduce per-token cost; Optimize will quantify potential savings.
[07:32] Markus Jansen: Any recommended quantization for our use? We're latency sensitive but also want accuracy for financial entities.
[07:40] Carlos Nguyen: For financial entity extraction and strict schema, we recommend full-precision model variants for p99-sensitive paths. For background tasks, q4 variants are a good tradeoff. We'll help simulate with your traffic in a POC.
[07:53] [08:00] Lena Ortiz: Are there known gotchas with KV cache and JSON mode? We've seen some stale context issues in other platforms.
[08:07] Carlos Nguyen: Good callout. Our KV cache is careful about prompt prefixes and cache keys include schema/version and route. So when you change your schema or prompt templates, the cache invalidates. Still, you should version your schemas in the Console.
[08:22] Priya Singh: For compliance we need audit exports and retention settings — is that per-account?
[08:28] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, retention is configurable per-account; enterprise plans can set retention to match compliance needs and export via S3 or SIEM.
[08:36] [08:45] Maya Patel: Quick pause — any other pressing questions while we run one more demo?
[08:50] Lena Ortiz: One more — how does Redwood handle hallucinated fields in the JSON?
[08:55] Carlos Nguyen: We tag hallucinations when schema validation fails or when the model returns unknown enum values. You can configure heuristics to treat unknowns as errors or to map them to a special 'unknown' enum value.
[09:07] [09:15] Carlos Nguyen: Ok last demo — structured output with embedded function calls. I'm going to show a two-step flow: the model suggests a payment, calls the function to create payment, then returns a confirmation object.
[09:28] [09:30] Carlos Nguyen: (typing) Running... stream shows function_call then webhook result is returned and the final JSON includes confirmation_id, created_at, and the _redwood_meta with latency_ms and model_version.
[09:44] Markus Jansen: That's clean. How do you surface model regressions over time?
[09:49] Maya Patel: We have Eval integrations — you can run automated prompt sets against new model builds. The Console tracks quality regressions and alerts if structured output metrics drop below thresholds.
[09:59] Priya Singh: Can the evals compare based on schema compliance rate?
[10:04] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — schema compliance, field-level accuracy, and custom metrics are supported. You can tie alerts to a rollout so a bad model never reaches 100% traffic.
[10:15] [10:20] Lena Ortiz: Great. Switching to integration questions — our internal audit wants to see example logs and the payloads stored. Is there a scrub/redaction feature?
[10:27] Carlos Nguyen: We provide redaction policies. You can configure which fields are redacted at rest, and which are allowed in logs. For payment tokens we recommend never logging full PANs and using masked fields.
[10:39] Maya Patel: Also we can run a short benchmark for you — Carlos, we have Markus's sample traffic later this week?
[10:45] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, Markus sent a sample of 10k requests earlier. We'll use that to estimate p95 latencies across Dedicated configs and to run a schema compliance pass.
[10:55] Markus Jansen: Yup I can make an expanded set with edge cases.
[10:59] [11:10] Lena Ortiz: On the commercial side, what's the path from POC to Dedicated?
[11:15] Maya Patel: Typical flow: 2-week POC on Dedicated or Hosted with dedicated pool, we produce a benchmark report and if it meets your SLOs we move to a reserved capacity contract. Pricing includes a base platform fee and usage above the commit.
[11:28] Priya Singh: Any penalties for switching to Private later? We may start Hosted then move to Private.
[11:34] Carlos Nguyen: No penalties — we support migration and data export. Private has a higher onboarding effort but we provide automation scripts and a partner for on-prem installs.
[11:45] [11:50] Lena Ortiz: Are there case studies for fintechs?
[11:53] Maya Patel: Yes — we'll share a couple of references and a win story about reduced unit cost with Optimize and strict schema enforcement preventing downstream errors.
[12:05] Carlos Nguyen: One more technical note — we surface model tokens and per-token cost by route and by token type in the Console, so you can see exactly where cost accumulates.
[12:16] Markus Jansen: That will help with chargebacks.
[12:20] [12:30] Priya Singh: Ok final bit — security review. We'll need SOC 2 Type II docs, ISO if available, and the KMS integration doc.
[12:39] Maya Patel: We'll send our SOC 2 report and the KMS guide; Carlos will attach the network diagrams.
[12:46] Carlos Nguyen: I'll also include the recommended mutual-TLS setup and example manifest for the webhook.
[12:53] [13:00] Lena Ortiz: Cool. For the POC we'd want 5% of traffic first then ramp.
[13:05] Maya Patel: Sounds good — we'll propose a rollout plan in the POC scope doc.
[13:10] Markus Jansen: On the function calling — do you support callbacks for async operations?
[13:16] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — the function call can return a job_id and Redwood can poll or accept a callback to synthesize the final structured output when complete.
[13:26] [13:30] Lena Ortiz: Any questions on our side?
[13:32] Priya Singh: Not right now, we just need to review the security materials.
[13:36] Maya Patel: Alright I'll recap the next steps at the end.
[13:40] [13:45] Carlos Nguyen: Quick demo note — sometimes transcripts have misrecognized acronyms, for example you might see "kv cash" instead of "KV cache". It's an artifact of transcription.
[13:55] Lena Ortiz: Haha, we've seen worse.
[14:00] [14:10] Maya Patel: Ok recap — action items: Maya will send recording, slides, SOC2; Carlos will prepare the POC scope and runbook and attach network diagrams; Markus will share extended sample traffic. POC kickoff target: week of 2025-06-23.
[14:28] Priya Singh: That timeline works for legal review.
[14:31] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone.
[14:33] Maya Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up via email with the docs and proposed POC plan. Bye!
[14:38] [14:40] End of recording.
